title: One name for the whole group
idea: A list gives many values a single name, replacing a pile of separate variables. Why that matters. Thinking-led.

exercises.prompt:
Compare these two ways to keep three scores:

A)  s1 = 8
     s2 = 5
     s3 = 9

B)  scores = [8, 5, 9]

What's the main advantage of B?
options: All three values share one name, as a group
B can only hold one value
exercises.explanation: In B, one name (scores) holds the whole group. That scales: three scores or three hundred, it's still one name.

exercises.prompt: Using a list means you don't need a brand-new variable name for every single value.
exercises.explanation: That's the whole point. One list name stands in for the entire group, however big it is.

exercises.prompt: You need to store the heights of 50 people. Which plan is sensible?
options: One list named heights holding all 50
One number that is the sum
exercises.explanation: Fifty variables would be a nightmare to manage. A single list named heights holds them all under one name.
The list prints as the whole group: [150, 162, 158]. One name, three values shown together.

exercises.prompt: Match each description to whether a single variable or a list fits best.
exercises.explanation: One value -> one variable. Many values of the same kind -> one list. Matching the tool to the shape of the data is a key skill.

exercises.prompt: A list counts as a single value you can store in one variable, even though it holds many items inside.
exercises.explanation: Yes — the list is one thing (one box) that happens to hold many items. You store the box under one name.

exercises.prompt: A problem says 'the rainfall for each of the 12 months.' What's the natural way to store it?
exercises.explanation: 'Each of the 12 months' is a group of 12 values — a perfect fit for one list of 12 numbers.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase in a problem most strongly suggests you should use a list?
exercises.explanation: 'All the players' is a whole group of values — that's a list. The others describe a single value.

exercises.prompt: Arrange these thinking steps for deciding how to store some data.
blocks: Read the problem and notice how many values it's about
If it's many values of the same kind, choose a list
Write the values into the list in order
exercises.explanation: First notice the shape (one value or many), then pick the tool (variable or list), then write it down.

exercises.prompt: You've learned WHY lists exist. What haven't we done yet with a list?
options: Reached in to grab one item by its position
Written a list in square brackets
Stored a list in a variable
exercises.explanation: We can make and print a list, but we can't yet pull out a single item. That's the very next unit.
